cards.front: Identify: title, artist, date, period/culture, medium, and what the symbols mean
cards.back:
Title: Melencolia I
Artist: Albrecht Dürer
Date: 1514
Period/Culture: Northern Renaissance, German
Medium/Technique: Engraving (a print)
Meaning: Self-portrait of the artistic temperament and creative paralysis (melancholy = a 'Saturnine' humor). A bat carries the title banner; hourglass = time running out; scattered tools = unused creativity; sleeping, underfed dog = neglected work; comet/flash of light = hope and inspiration ahead.

Definition: Pigment mixed with oil (linseed); slow drying allows layered glazes, rich color, fine detail. Perfected in the North.
Applies to: Last Supper (oil and tempera); Northern Renaissance painting generally

Definition: Image made by transferring ink from a prepared block or plate onto paper; reproducible many times.
Applies to: Melencolia I

Definition: Relief print: cut away wood around the lines, ink the raised surface, press onto paper.
Applies to: No focus work. Contrast: Melencolia I is an engraving, not a woodcut

Definition: Intaglio print: lines cut into a metal (copper) plate with a burin; ink fills the grooves. Finer lines than woodcut.
Applies to: Melencolia I

cards.front: Northern Renaissance: where, and what was society like?
cards.back:
Where: Western Europe (Flanders, Holy Roman Empire)
Society: Thriving commerce, migration to cities, powerful merchant and banker patrons
Guilds: Organized artists, controlling clients, wages, and apprenticeships

cards.front: Protestant Reformation: when, and what did it do to art?
cards.back:
When: 1517
Effect: Iconoclasm (image-breaking); patronage shifted away from the Catholic Church and the role of religious images changed

cards.front: Name the 6 characteristics of Northern Renaissance art.
cards.back:
One: Extreme detail (wood grain, reflections, textiles)
Two: Oil paint for fine, layered detail
Three: Donors shown inside religious scenes
Four: Contemporary local settings for biblical scenes
Five: Genre scenes of everyday life, often with a moral
Six: Iconography: objects as symbols (dog = fidelity, candle = divine presence)

cards.front: Jan van Eyck, Ghent Altarpiece: key facts.
cards.back:
Date: 1423 (per lecture)
Medium: Oil on wood; large triptych, about 11.5 x 7.5 ft
Exterior: Annunciation in a contemporary Flemish city; figures in grisaille (gray) to imitate stone; kneeling donors in full color
Interior: God enthroned, Mary as Queen of Heaven, Adam and Eve, Lamb of God (original sin to Christ's sacrifice)
Details: Brooch reflects a chapel window; pelican piercing its chest = Christ's sacrifice; targeted by the Nazis in WWII

cards.front: Jan van Eyck, Giovanni Arnolfini and His Wife: key facts and symbols.
cards.back:
Date: 1434, oil on wood
Function: Debated: portrait vs. legal marriage document
Dog: Loyalty and fidelity in marriage
Pattens removed: Entering a sacred space
One lit candle: Divine presence blessing the union
Saint Margaret on the bedpost: Patron saint of childbirth (fertility)
Mirror: Reflects two witnesses; signature "Johannes de Eyck fuit hic" above it, maybe naming the artist as a witness

cards.front: Woodcut vs. engraving: how do they differ?
cards.back:
Woodcut: Wood carved away around the lines; bold, coloring-book-like lines
Engraving: Lines cut into a metal plate; ink fills the grooves; finer lines and more gradation
First printed book: Gutenberg Bible, 1455

cards.front: Albrecht Dürer: who was he, and what made him different?
cards.back:
Who: Painter and printmaker in Nuremberg, Holy Roman Empire; the celebrity artist of his era
Brand: Used his A.D. monogram as a logo and claimed his work as intellectual property
Rhinoceros: Drew it from a description, never saw one, so it has armor and turtle-like legs; shows how exploration news spread through prints
